passages.t: Egypt comes and goes, and the Chaldeans will return
passages.happening:
Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah son of Josiah king in place of Coniah (verse 1). ‘But he and his officers and the people of the land refused to obey the words that the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah the prophet’ (verse 2). Yet Zedekiah sends Jehucal and the priest Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for them (verse 3). Jeremiah is still free to come and go (verse 4).

Pharaoh's army has left Egypt, and the Chaldeans besieging Jerusalem have heard and withdrawn (verse 5). God tells Jeremiah to answer the king that Pharaoh's army, which came out to help, will go back to Egypt (verse 7). The Chaldeans will return, capture the city and burn it (verse 8). They must not deceive themselves that the Chaldeans are gone for good (verse 9). Even if Judah struck down the whole Chaldean army and only wounded men were left in their tents, those men would get up and burn the city (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
After Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 597 BC and deported Jehoiachin, he made Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah king and renamed him Zedekiah. Zedekiah later rebelled, trusting in Egypt, and the siege began.

The Egyptian army's march, which chapter 34 also mentions, forced the Babylonians to lift the siege for a time. To the people in Jerusalem it must have looked like the answer to their prayers. Jeremiah said it was only a pause.

Clay letters found in 1935 at Lachish come from these same months. One reports that a Judean commander named Konyahu son of Elnathan had gone down to Egypt, which fits a Judah looking to Egypt for help.

Zedekiah wanted Jeremiah's prayers but not his message. He asked for help without being willing to obey.
passages.later: Isaiah had warned of the same trust a century before: ‘Egypt’s help is futile and empty’ (Isaiah 30:7). Kings records Zedekiah's appointment: the king of Babylon ‘made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in his place’ (2 Kings 24:17).
passages.asks: Zedekiah asked for prayer but would not listen to the answer. Ask whether you ask God for help while ignoring what he has already said. And ask what lull in your troubles you have mistaken for the end of them.

passages.t: Arrested at the gate, and a secret question
passages.happening:
While the Chaldean army is away, Jeremiah sets out from Jerusalem to the land of Benjamin to claim his share of property there (verses 11 and 12). At the Benjamin Gate the officer of the guard, Irijah, arrests him, saying he is deserting to the Chaldeans (verse 13). Jeremiah says it is a lie, but Irijah will not listen and brings him to the officials (verse 14). They are angry, beat him and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe (verse 15). He stays a long time in a cell in the dungeon (verse 16).

Later King Zedekiah sends for him and asks him privately in the palace whether there is any word from the LORD. Jeremiah says there is: the king will be handed to the king of Babylon (verse 17). Then he asks what wrong he has done that they have imprisoned him (verse 18). Where now are the prophets who said Babylon would not come (verse 19)? He begs not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die there (verse 20).

Zedekiah orders him kept in the courtyard of the guard and given a loaf of bread each day from the bakers' street, until all the bread in the city is gone (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Jeremiah's trip to Benjamin was probably connected with family property, perhaps the same land at Anathoth that chapter 32 describes. To a guard at the gate, a man who had preached surrender walking toward the enemy looked like a deserter.

The private meeting is telling. The king could not be seen consulting Jeremiah in public, but he wanted to know. Jeremiah gave him the same word in secret as in public.

The courtyard of the guard was a lighter confinement than the dungeon. The daily loaf from the bakers' street kept Jeremiah alive while food ran out in the city. The detail until all the bread in the city was gone shows how long the siege lasted.
passages.later: Jeremiah stayed in the courtyard of the guard, where he later bought the field at Anathoth (Jeremiah 32:2). Kings records how the bread did run out: ‘the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food’ (2 Kings 25:3).
passages.asks: Jeremiah gave the king the same word in private as in public. Ask whether what you say about God changes depending on who is listening. And ask how you would hold on to truth when it has already cost you your freedom.
